title: Strong Sense of Identity Linked to Mental Well-Being
paragraphs: Many people think that a person's identity, or their sense of who they are, is mostly formed in their teenage years and early adulthood. However, a long-term study from Finland suggests that identity continues to develop well into adulthood, and that a stronger sense of identity is linked to better mental well-being.

The study was carried out by researchers at the University of Jyväskylä, led by doctoral researcher Liinu Marin, and published in the Journal of Adult Development in 2026. It used data from the Jyväskylä Longitudinal Study of Personality and Social Development, which has followed the same group of people for more than 50 years, since 1968.

The researchers measured the participants' identity at the ages of 27, 36, 42, 50 and 61. They looked at how firmly people were committed to their views in different areas of life, and whether they had formed these views by exploring options for themselves or had simply adopted them from other people or society. The researchers also measured the participants' mental well-being, including their sense of purpose in life, their feeling of connection to their communities, their satisfaction with life and any feelings of anxiety or depression.

The results showed that the participants' identities continued to develop in a positive direction between the ages of 27 and 61, although most of the change took place between 27 and 42. According to Marin, this shows that identity can continue to develop throughout adulthood.

In addition, the researchers found that people with a more positively developed identity tended to have better mental well-being. For example, they had better psychological and social well-being and fewer feelings of anxiety.

However, the study did not examine which factor affects the other. As Marin pointed out, it is possible that good mental well-being also helps people develop their identity, so the link may work in both directions.
Other studies published in 2026 have also found that a positive sense of identity may help protect young people against depression.
